# Ārāmadūsakajātaka (Ja 46)

**ID:** Ja 46
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Ārāmadūsakajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The One Who Spoiled a Park
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja46
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ārāmadūsakajātaka* (Ja 46) is a narrative belonging to the Pali *Jātaka* collection [SuttaCentral; Anandajoti 2010]. The framing "story of the present" relates that while traveling in a village in Kosala, the Buddha and his monastic assembly were offered a meal in a park by a local landowner, prompting the Buddha to deliver this discourse concerning a village youth who had ruined the grounds [SuttaCentral; Appleton 2010; Fausbøll 1877]. In the embedded "story of the past," a king leaves a troupe of monkeys in charge of watering young saplings during a festival; eager to conserve water, the monkeys pull up every sapling to measure the length of its roots before watering, thereby destroying the entire orchard [Anandajoti 2010; Appleton 2010].

A wise observer (*paṇḍitapuriso*) who plays no active role in the events utters the canonical verse (*Na ve anatthakusalena...*) as an aphoristic reflection on the scene, observing that an unskilled fool seeking to do good or achieving position merely brings ruin upon himself and others [Anandajoti 2010; Appleton 2010; Fausbøll 1877]. In the *samodhāna* (re-identification of characters), the Buddha reveals that the park-spoiling village boy was the monkey leader of the past, while the wise man was the Bodhisatta [Appleton 2010; Fausbøll 1877]. Naomi Appleton observes that the verse lacks overtly Buddhist doctrine and functions as a moral adage, while visual depictions of the monkeys pulling up sapling roots appear in ancient Indian art at Bhārhut as well as throughout South and Southeast Asian temple iconography [Appleton 2010].

Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus records any Pali-internal text reuse or cross-language parallels for this jātaka in other Buddhist corpora [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral catalogs six modern translations across four languages, including an English rendering by Bhikkhu Sujato [SuttaCentral].
